transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-05
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Priya Desai (Redwood), Marco Reyes (Redwood SE), Dana Patel (BrightPath - Head of ML), Eric Nguyen (BrightPath - Infra), Sarah Lopez (BrightPath - Security)

Summary:
Customer is evaluating where to place safety filters / moderation relative to generation to minimize latency/throughput impact while satisfying healthcare compliance and auditability. They want concrete numbers and recommended architectures for VPC/on-prem pilots.

[00:00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing this in. Today Marco and I want to walk through tradeoffs when you put moderation or safety filters in front of, inline with, or after generation and the runtime implications — batching, kv cache interactions, quantization, etc. Dana, Eric, Sarah, thanks for the context you sent over.

[00:00:28] Dana: Yeah thanks, quick background — BrightPath is building a clinician assistant, gen-AI driven summaries of patient notes. Major concerns are PII leakage, hallucinations, and meeting our internal audit bar. Latency target is 500ms p50 and 1s p95 for short prompts, throughput target ~200 reqs/s initially. We're exploring dedicated or VPC private options.

[00:00:54] Marco: Great. So at a high level there are three pattern archetypes we usually see for moderation placement: pre-filter (client or edge), inline synchronous moderation (blocking generation until check completes), and post-filter (async scan after generation). Each has performance and safety tradeoffs.

[00:01:17] Sarah: And we care about provable blocking for certain categories — e.g., PHI exfiltration — so async post-filter alone might not be sufficient unless we have guaranteed rollback.

[00:01:36] Marco: Right. Quick perf notes: pre-filter is cheapest for latency because you can drop obviously disallowed content before we touch the LLM; it can run on CPU or on a cheap endpoint. But pre-filters have false negatives — subtle PII might slip through. Inline moderation means every request is scanned before or as part of generation; that adds CPU work and can increase tail latency, especially if moderation is synchronous and not batched. Post-filter pushes cost to after generation which reduces initial latency but increases downstream remediation complexity and cost.

[00:02:10] Eric: How much latency are we talking when moderation runs inline? If we run a model-based classifier on the same GPU as the generator, what's the overhead?

[00:02:22] Marco: Good question. Two sub-cases: a) run classifier on CPU or small CPU instance — cheap but slow (100-300ms depending on model and input length); b) run a lightweight GPU-optimized classifier — if you colocate on the same GPU and pipeline it correctly you can amortize some cost but it can evict KV cache or contention with generation kernels. In our benchmarks, an optimized classifier at 8-bit can add ~50-120ms median overhead when pipelined, but the p95 can spike if batching isn't aligned. If the classifier runs as a separate GPU pod you can parallelize but you add network hop/time.

[00:03:02] Dana: You mentioned KV cache eviction — can you expand? We're relying on KV caching to hit latency targets for multi-turn notes.

[00:03:10] Marco: Sure. KV cache lives in GPU memory for active sessions to avoid recomputing key/values. If you run additional GPU workloads on the same device or reinitialize sessions for moderation checks, you risk evicting or invalidating KV pages, which hurts subsequent token latencies. For example, a heavy classifier that allocates memory can cause cache thrashing and then the next generation call has to rebuild the cache, adding 100ms-200ms depending on prefix length.

[00:03:38] Priya: So placement-wise, if your workload is very latency sensitive, we often recommend a hybrid: cheap heuristic pre-filter + async GPU classifier for high-risk cases, and for categories that must be blocked (PHI) run a synchronous, fast rule-based check inline. That way you catch the obvious stuff early and only escalate ambiguous cases.

[00:04:05] Sarah: Is that hybrid approach compatible with regulatory audit logs and provable decisions? We need traceability for every blocked request.

[00:04:14] Marco: Yes — Redwood can log moderation decisions in the control plane with immutable audit entries. For VPC/private deployments we can stream encrypted audit logs to your KMS-backed storage. We'll include those details in the security appendix.

[00:04:33] Eric: What about batching? We rely on continuous batching for cost efficiency — how do moderation steps affect batching behavior and throughput?

[00:04:43] Marco: Moderation can either be batched or act as a gating stage that breaks batches. If moderation is synchronous and per-request, it can reduce batch sizes and hurt throughput. For high throughput, we recommend: pre-filter to let many requests pass, queue ambiguous ones to a batched classifier (so classifier runs on micro-batches), and let generation run on optimized batches. Also, you can use batching windows — e.g., hold for 10-20ms to build a batch — but that increases p50 slightly. There's a tradeoff between cost and p95 latency.

[00:05:18] Dana: We're also using quantized models (4-bit) for cost reasons. Any gotchas for running classifiers or moderation with quantized generators?

[00:05:28] Marco: Quantization affects model performance and sometimes classification accuracy if you quantize the classifier too aggressively. Generator quantization mainly impacts throughput and memory; classifiers should be kept higher precision if you need high accuracy. On the runtime level, mixed quantization can cause different kernel paths — sometimes leading to head-of-line issues if you try to colocate a float16 classifier with 4-bit generator on the same device. Our runtime isolates kernels and schedules to minimize interference, but isolation is not perfect. Recommended: run classifier on a small float16 pod or CPU-backed endpoint and keep your generator quantized.

[00:06:05] Sarah: For the blocking categories, we need zero-tolerance. Is there a pattern to guarantee zero exposure before generation?

[00:06:15] Priya: The only practical zero-exposure pattern is strict client-side redaction for known PII fields plus an inline deterministic rule-based check server-side before generation. Anything model-based has some FnR/Fp tradeoffs. Deterministic checks (regex, schema validators) are fast and can be synchronous with near-zero latency. Then you can layer model-based checks for fuzzy cases as an additional guard.

[00:06:43] Eric: If we do synchronous checks and they cause latency spikes at p95, can Redwood route traffic to a cheaper fallback model or degrade gracefully?

[00:06:52] Marco: Yes — smart routing policies are a key capability. You can configure policy: if synchronous moderation queue > X ms or GPU utilization high, route to a smaller generator model or to a cached summarization for non-critical flows. That reduces tail latency but changes fidelity. We can set canary rules and A/B to measure impact.

[00:07:15] Dana: Let's talk numbers — can you estimate added cost per 1k requests for a hybrid approach versus pure post-filtering?

[00:07:25] Marco: High-level: pure post-filtering is lowest immediate cost per request because many cheaper requests don't pay for classifier before generation, but remediation and rollback costs can be high. Hybrid with pre-filter + batched model classifier tends to add $0.50-$2 per 1k requests depending on classifier size and batch efficiency on GPUs; this is rough and depends on throughput and batching efficiency. We'll run a cost model with your sample traffic.

[00:07:53] Sarah: How do streaming responses interact with moderation? We stream partial tokens to the UI for speed. If moderation blocks mid-stream, how do we prevent leakage?

[00:08:03] Marco: Streaming complicates things. Two options: a) don't stream until moderation check passes — which adds latency but is safest; b) stream optimistically but implement immediate revocation (server signals client to redact) — however, once tokens are sent to client browsers, you can't truly retract. For healthcare, we recommend not streaming PHI-containing outputs until checks complete. For non-PHI flows you can stream with optimistic heuristics.

[00:08:33] Eric: For our pilot in VPC, we'd like to benchmark two variants: inline sync classifier colocated vs pre-filter + batched classifier. Can Redwood provide an infra template for the Dedicated pilot?

[00:08:44] Priya: Yes — action item: Marco will provision a Dedicated pilot infra template with recommended CPU/GPU sizing, batching windows, and a baseline moderation classifier config. We'll include scripts to reproduce latency/throughput experiments.

[00:08:59] Dana: Also include variation with and without KV cache warming and cold-starts. Those cold-start times are our real pain point in the clinic.

[00:09:07] Marco: Absolutely. We'll show impact of cache misses, memory pressure scenarios, and quantization profiles. We'll instrument trace hooks so you can see where time is spent (moderation, gen, transfer, decoding).

[00:09:22] Sarah: In terms of compliance, we need audit logs for every moderation decision and immutable evidence for blocked items. Can we get that in the VPC flow?

[00:09:30] Priya: Yes — in VPC/private deployments we stream encrypted audit logs to your S3/GCS or into your SIEM using syslog/forwarder. We'll also support signed attestations for decision snapshots. We'll attach the security appendix to the follow-up email.

[00:09:49] Eric: Any recommendations on model selection for the classifier? Open-source vs Redwood-curated?

[00:09:57] Marco: For classifiers we often recommend smaller, high-precision float16 models or dedicated discriminators that were trained for your taxonomy. Redwood has curated classifier models verified for moderation tasks. If you want custom rules, you can fine-tune or use few-shot prompts, but that usually increases variability. We can seed with our curated models and then fine-tune with your labeled edge cases.

[00:10:19] Dana: How do you handle false positives that block clinician workflow — i.e., we can't have too many false blocks?

[00:10:28] Marco: Good point. There's a UX pattern: allow a soft-block with override + logging for low-risk false positives. For high-risk categories (PHI exfiltration) we do hard-blocks. Also we can set thresholds per category, and route to a human review queue for ambiguous items. We'll instrument false-positive rates and surface them in Redwood Console.

[00:10:50] Priya: We're now about to demo the planned benchmark and sample traces. Marco, do you want to walk through the sample trace we prepared?

[00:10:58] Marco: Yep. (screen share) This trace shows a 3-step flow: client pre-filter -> generator request (quantized model, cached KV) -> batched classifier for ambiguous cases. Notice the p50 is 380ms, p95 920ms. When we switch to synchronous classifier on the same GPU without careful batching, p95 jumps to 1.4s and cost increases ~20%. Also see the cache-thrashing example where a classifier pod briefly allocates memory causing a 180ms penalty to next request.

[00:11:40] Dana: That aligns with our observations. Any notes on how to tune batching windows to minimize p95 while maintaining throughput?

[00:11:49] Marco: Sure. Tuning knobs: batching window (ms), max batch size, priority queuing for small low-latency requests, and separate pools for short-vs-long sequences. For example, 10ms window with priority preemption will keep p50 low and still get reasonable batch sizes. For your traffic profile we recommend an aggressive priority queue with a 10-15ms batching window for short requests.

[00:12:18] Sarah: On logging and audit, we also need RBAC so only certain roles can see raw outputs. Does Redwood support redaction and role-based access?

[00:12:27] Priya: Yes — RBAC and field-level redaction are supported in Private deployments; we can redact PII in logs and only surface metadata to non-privileged roles. We'll document the configuration options.

[00:12:40] Eric: For cost modeling, we need a sample of 1M requests/month, 40% short (<128 tokens), 60% medium (128-512). Can you run a cost projection for hybrid vs post-filter?

[00:12:52] Marco: We'll run that. Action item noted. Our initial estimate will include GPU hours for generation, classifier cost, and expected cache hit ratios.

[00:13:04] Dana: One last runbook question — if a moderation model drifts, can we hot-swap or rollback without service interruption?

[00:13:13] Marco: Yes — we support canary deploys for classifiers and generators, with automatic rollback on performance or quality regressions. You can pin versions at route-level and use A/B. Redwood Console will surface eval metrics.

[00:13:26] Priya: Great. To recap next steps: we'll send the security appendix and design doc, Marco will provision the Dedicated pilot template and run benchmarks with your sample prompts, and Dana/Eric will share traffic and labels. We'll aim to kick off the pilot the week of 2025-06-16.

[00:13:45] Dana: Sounds good. Appreciate the pragmatic guidance — this hybrid approach feels actionable.

[00:13:53] Priya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and the calendar invite.

[00:14:00] (meeting ends)
